text: Separation of duties is the principle that no single person should hold two permissions that, combined, let them carry out fraud or a serious error entirely on their own. If one person can both initiate an action and approve that same action, there's no second set of eyes anywhere in the process - the control that approval is supposed to provide simply doesn't exist.

A toxic combination is a specific, named pairing of permissions that creates an SoD violation when one person holds both. Neither permission has to be dangerous by itself - the risk lives entirely in the pairing. Identity governance teams maintain a catalog of these known combinations and check real access against it, rather than relying on anyone spotting the problem by eye.

The textbook example: create-vendor plus approve-payment. A clerk who can only create vendor records needs someone else to approve any payment to them. A manager who can only approve payments can't invent a vendor to pay in the first place. But one person holding both can create a vendor controlled by an accomplice and then approve a payment to it themselves - a complete fraud cycle with zero external review. It's a standard example in SOX internal-controls guidance precisely because it's simple to execute and easy to prevent, if anyone checks.

The same structural problem shows up elsewhere: creating a purchase order plus confirming the goods arrived enables a fictitious purchase. Editing a payroll record plus approving the payroll run lets someone change a pay rate and pay it out themselves. And an IT admin who can both grant access and certify that same access removes the independent check a certification campaign is supposed to provide.

SoD has to be checked across a person's total access, not one system at a time - someone with approve-payment rights in the ERP and a separate database login that edits the vendor table directly still has the same toxic combination, even though no single system's permission list shows it. Catching that at scale, across every system, is exactly what purpose-built identity governance tooling is built for - that's Lesson 24.
